summary.headline: A real turnaround, but borrowings nearly doubled in six months and the price assumes today's high returns last for decades
summary.text: Swisstek (Ceylon) PLC (PARQ.N0000), the Vallibel group's tile-grout and adhesives maker that also owns 68% of Swisstek Aluminium, has turned around strongly: EPS went from a loss in 2023/24 to Rs 7.32 in 2025/26, and the six months to September 2026 were up another 8% (EPS Rs 3.05). But the September quarter's profit fell 18% as administrative costs more than doubled, and borrowings jumped to Rs 9.16bn from Rs 5.72bn in March as stock was built up and suppliers were paid down: net debt is now 1.75x equity and operating cash was Rs 3.1bn negative in the half. That debt and a record of losses in 2022/23 and 2023/24 make the share risky, so the required return is high (22.3%). At Rs 86.30 the share trades at 2.8x NAV (Rs 31.06) and 11.5x trailing earnings; on today's ROE fading to a long-run 19%, the methods put fair value at about Rs 27.50, so the price is about three times that. I'd buy only at up to about Rs 23.40 and treat under Rs 20.70 as a strong buy: in practice, not a share to buy at today's price.

valuation.note: Fair value weights the bear/base/bull averages of three methods 30/50/20: Rs 18.33 / 27.68 / 41.02, giving Rs 27.55 (0.89x NAV). The methods are justified price to book, P/E and residual income, all from scripts/valuation.py at a 22.3% cost of equity. A whole-company DCF and a dividend model were run but not weighted (see the methods note).

fullText:
Summary: Swisstek (Ceylon) PLC (PARQ.N0000), the Vallibel group's tile-grout and adhesives maker that also owns 68% of Swisstek Aluminium, has turned around strongly: EPS went from a loss in 2023/24 to Rs 7.32 in 2025/26, and the six months to September 2026 were up another 8% (EPS Rs 3.05). But the September quarter's profit fell 18% as administrative costs more than doubled, and borrowings jumped to Rs 9.16bn from Rs 5.72bn in March as stock was built up and suppliers were paid down: net debt is now 1.75x equity and operating cash was Rs 3.1bn negative in the half. That debt and a record of losses in 2022/23 and 2023/24 make the share risky, so the required return is high (22.3%). At Rs 86.30 the share trades at 2.8x NAV (Rs 31.06) and 11.5x trailing earnings; on today's ROE fading to a long-run 19%, the methods put fair value at about Rs 27.50, so the price is about three times that. I'd buy only at up to about Rs 23.40 and treat under Rs 20.70 as a strong buy: in practice, not a share to buy at today's price.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 86.30 (CSE close, 20 November 2026). Please check it live. It traded at Rs 68.00–86.50 in April–June 2026 and Rs 67.10–86.00 in July–September 2026; Rs 42.00–112.50 in the year to March 2026, which closed at Rs 79.50.
Six months to 30 September 2026 (group, unaudited): sales up 8.1% to Rs 8.66bn; gross margin 27.9% (23.1%); profit from operations Rs 1.05bn (+14%); net finance costs Rs 375mn (Rs 278mn); profit attributable Rs 418mn (+7.6%); EPS Rs 3.05 (Rs 2.84). The June quarter was strong (EPS Rs 1.61, +50%); the September quarter weak (EPS Rs 1.44 against Rs 1.76) as sales grew only 1.6%, administrative costs rose to Rs 447mn from Rs 182mn and finance costs rose. Stock provisions of Rs 147mn were charged in the half.
Segments (six months): tile grout, adhesives and flooring sales up 25% to Rs 2.60bn (profit before tax Rs 344mn); aluminium (Swisstek Aluminium, 68% owned) up 2.1% to Rs 6.06bn (Rs 318mn).
Year to March 2026 (audited): revenue Rs 16.88bn (+10.6%: aluminium Rs 12.31bn, tile products Rs 3.98bn, zinc-aluminium roofing Rs 0.42bn, doubled), gross margin 25.4% (22.6%), profit attributable Rs 1.00bn (+16%), EPS Rs 7.32 (Rs 6.32), dividends Rs 2.05 (28% of profit), NAV Rs 28.40, operating cash Rs 1.41bn (−Rs 0.005bn the year before). Rs 202mn of group profit belonged to the outside holders of Swisstek Aluminium.
Debt: borrowings Rs 9.16bn at September 2026 (Rs 5.72bn in March), of which short-term loans Rs 5.53bn and overdrafts Rs 1.22bn; leases Rs 0.16bn; cash Rs 0.49bn; net debt Rs 8.83bn, 1.75x equity (1.13x in March). Operating cash was −Rs 3.12bn in the half as stock rose Rs 1.2bn, receivables Rs 0.76bn, and payables fell Rs 1.9bn.
Cycle: group profit Rs 900mn (2021/22), a loss of Rs 703mn (2022/23, when finance costs reached Rs 2.04bn), a loss of Rs 113mn (2023/24, EPS Rs −0.51), then EPS Rs 6.32 (2024/25) and Rs 7.32 (2025/26).

Management and plans
Management wants growth from roofing, waterproofing, DIY and new export markets with little new plant (capacity already 95% used) and promised tighter stock and less short-term debt, but in the first half of 2026/27 short-term loans more than doubled. In 2025/26 capex was Rs 393mn (1.4x depreciation), mainly buildings, a grout packing machine and a vehicle; capex in the first half of 2026/27 was already Rs 371mn. Plans include roofing, timber flooring, a DIY range, waterproofing, a construction-services business, possibly buying a local plant, and selling aluminium beyond the US. The promise to rely less on short-term loans was missed in the first half.

Shareholders
Lanka Tiles (47.8%), Lanka Walltiles (11.5%) and Royal Ceramics (6.9%), all Vallibel One group companies, together hold 66.2% and control Swisstek. The September quarter's moves were small: People's Leasing/Dr K A P Gunawardhana added 0.51mn shares (now 2.57%) and DFCC Bank A/C 02 0.28mn (now 1.00%). The public holds 30.7% (5,035 holders). Directors hold almost nothing (Mr. A M Weerasinghe 263,142 shares).

Required return
Cost of equity 22.3% (bear 23.8%, bull 20.8%): risk-free 8.24% + beta 1.37 × (4.2% + 6.08%). The beta is a Building Materials unlevered 0.90 relevered for net debt at 0.75x market value; it's high because of the debt. WACC 15.8% (debt weight 42.8%, cost of debt 9.64%).

Methods
NAV (Rs 31.06): the price is 2.8x.
Return on equity: 26% in 2025/26 and 32% in 2024/25, after losses in the two years before; five-year average about 14%.
P/E: 11.5x trailing EPS of Rs 7.53.
Dividends: Rs 2.05 for 2025/26, a 2.4% yield, covered 3.9x by cash after maintenance capex.
Justified price to book: Rs 15.69 / 25.14 / 37.78, weighted Rs 24.83.
P/E method (justified P/E 3.6 / 4.3 / 5.1x on EPS of Rs 6.05 / 7.05 / 7.75): Rs 21.83 / 30.03 / 39.27, weighted Rs 29.42.
Residual income: Rs 17.48 / 27.88 / 46.01, weighted Rs 28.39.
Three methods are weighted: justified price to book, P/E and residual income. A whole-company DCF was run (scripts/reinvestment.py): start cash Rs 0.84 / 1.20 / 1.56bn (operating cash plus after-tax interest, less maintenance capex of Rs 0.30–0.33bn; bear the 2024/25–2025/26 average, bull 2025/26 alone, base between), growth 3% / 5% / 7% for five years then 4% / 5% / 6%, return on new capital 14% / 17% / 20%, at WACC 16.6% / 15.8% / 14.9%. Firm values of Rs 3.8 / 7.1 / 12.5bn against net debt of Rs 8.83bn give Rs −36.5 / −12.7 / +26.6 a share (51–69% of the value comes after year 5), before taking off the 32% of Swisstek Aluminium owned by others. It isn't weighted because operating cash swings by billions with stock and supplier credit (−Rs 0.005bn in 2024/25, +Rs 1.41bn in 2025/26, −Rs 3.12bn in the half to September) and September's net debt includes a seasonal stock build; at March's Rs 5.21bn the base case would be about Rs 14 a share. Still, it's a warning that the debt takes most of the business's value. A dividend model gives Rs 8–15 and isn't weighted either: the payout is 28% of profit, so it understates value. Growth check: assumed 3% / 5% / 7% against 5.1% supported (29% of after-tax operating profit reinvested × 17.4% return on capital); all within 2 points. R&D is Rs 6mn (0.04% of revenue), so no R&D adjustment. 2025/26 capex of Rs 393mn was 1.4x depreciation, mostly upkeep and buildings, not a big expansion; capacity is 95% used, so faster growth would need new plant.

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity: 23.8% / 22.3% / 20.8%.
Long-run ROE: 14% / 19% / 24% (five-year average about 14%, last two years 26–32%).
Long-term growth: 4% / 5% / 6% (below the 12.24% bond yield and WACC).
EPS for the year to March 2027: Rs 6.05 / 7.05 / 7.75 (H1 Rs 3.05; second half Rs 3.00 / 4.00 / 4.70 against Rs 4.48 last year).
Growth for the next five years: 3% / 5% / 7%, against 5.1% supported.
Average of the three methods: Rs 18.33 / 27.68 / 41.02.

Fair value and buy price
Fair value: weighting 30/50/20 gives Rs 27.55 (0.89x NAV), so Rs 86.30 is about 213% above it.
Buy price: a 15% margin of safety gives Rs 23.41, and 25% gives Rs 20.66.
Plan for 500 shares: 200 at up to Rs 27.55, 150 at up to Rs 23.41 and 150 at up to Rs 20.66. That averages about Rs 24.24, about Rs 12,120, against Rs 43,150 at Rs 86.30.
Realism: Rs 27.55 needs a fall of about 68%. The share has traded at Rs 67.10–86.50 since April 2026 and its low in the year to March 2026 was Rs 42.00; it was last below Rs 28 in 2024 (Rs 19.10 at March 2024), before the turnaround. Not realistic unless profits slump again.

Sensitivity (residual income base case, Rs per share; long-run growth 5%)
Cost of equity 20.8%: 21.7 / 32.2 / 45.7 for long-run ROE of 14% / 19% / 24%.
Cost of equity 22.3%: 19.2 / 27.9 / 39.0.
Cost of equity 23.8%: 17.1 / 24.4 / 33.7.
The required return matters most. At the 17% used in the first analysis, the three methods would give a fair value of about Rs 43.60; at 20%, about Rs 32.90. At 22.3%, today's Rs 86.30 needs ROE of about 38% for ever.

What would change my view
Supports a higher value: Borrowings falling back towards March's Rs 5.7bn as stock is sold; ROE holding above 25% through a full cycle; Tile, roofing and waterproofing sales growing 20%+ a year; Lower interest rates, cutting the required return.
Supports a lower value: Profit falling further after the weak September quarter; Administrative costs staying at the new level; Borrowings staying above Rs 9bn, or more stock write-downs; Aluminium prices or export demand falling; A return to the losses of 2022–2024.

Business tests: 1 of 4 passed (return on equity). Fails: net debt 1.75x equity, losses in 2022/23 and 2023/24, uneven cash flow. Category 3, avoid for now (unchanged).

These are estimates from the annual report to March 2026 and the interim reports to June and September 2026. The interim figures are unaudited, so check the price before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
